engines.body: Foot placement, weight distribution, spine alignment, knee bend
engines.mind: Understanding WHY this position works — geometry, not just instruction
engines.emotion: First moment of 'I feel stable' — confidence from structure

audience.hook: Every punch, every slip, every step starts from the same place. Get this wrong and nothing else works.
audience.question: Why does stance matter more than any punch?

core.thesis: The stance is not a starting position — it's the operating system. Every movement in boxing is an extension of stance, and every mistake traces back to it.
keyPoints: Stance is the foundation — not something you learn once and forget, something you return to constantly
Foot width: shoulder-width base. Too narrow = no balance. Too wide = no mobility.
Weight distribution: roughly 50/50, slight forward bias. Ready to move in any direction.
Lead foot points toward opponent, rear foot at ~45 degrees
Knees slightly bent — springs loaded, never locked
Upright posture: Cuban style. Not crouched, not leaning. Spine stacked.
Hands up, chin down, elbows in — but that comes from guard (lesson 4). Stance is feet first.
The stance test: can you move any direction instantly without adjusting first? If not, your stance is wrong.
commonMisconceptions: Stance is boring / basic — it's the most important thing in boxing and the first thing that breaks under pressure
You learn stance in session 1 and move on — even professionals drill stance
Wider is more stable — wider kills your mobility
Copying a pro's stance works — your body is different, the principles are the same but the measurements adapt

coachEye.observe: Watch the rear heel — is it planted or floating? Floating = not committed, planted = loaded
coachEye.compare: Same student, hands-down relaxed stance vs fighting stance — how much did their balance actually change?
coachEye.predict: A student with locked knees will fall off balance on their first cross. Every time.
coachEye.diagnose: If a punch has no power, check the feet before checking the hands. It's almost always the feet.

scenes.title: Everything Starts Here
scenes.narration: Before the jab. Before the guard. Before footwork. There's the stance. Get this right and everything else gets easier. Get this wrong and nothing else works.

scenes.title: The Feet
scenes.narration: Shoulder-width apart. Lead foot pointing forward. Rear foot at forty-five degrees. Knees bent — springs loaded, never locked. This is your base. Everything you do in boxing is an extension of this position.

scenes.title: Weight Distribution
scenes.narration: Fifty-fifty. Ready to move in any direction without shifting first. Too much weight forward — you can't retreat. Too much weight back — your punches have nothing behind them.

scenes.title: Upright
scenes.narration: Cuban stance is upright. Not crouched. Not leaning. Spine stacked over hips. This isn't a choice — it's physics. An upright spine gives you rotation, vision, and the ability to move your feet without resetting.
scenes.learningObjective: Upright posture — Cuban style vs crouch

scenes.title: The Test
scenes.narration: Here's how you know your stance is right. Can you move forward, back, left, or right — instantly — without adjusting first? If you have to shift your weight before you move, your stance is wrong.

scenes.title: It Never Stops
scenes.narration: Beginners learn stance. Professionals drill stance. The difference between a good boxer and a great one often comes down to whether their stance holds under pressure. This is lesson three — and it's the lesson you'll practice longest.

reel.hook: If a punch has no power, don't check the hands. Check the feet.
reel.cta: The stance is everything. Learn it right.

checkpoints: Can you move any direction without adjusting first?
Is your rear heel floating or planted?
Are your knees bent or locked?

teachingCues: Don't correct hands in session 1 — get the feet right first. Guard is lesson 4.
Use the 'push test': gently push the student's shoulder. If they stumble, stance needs work.
Ask students to close their eyes in stance — if they sway, weight distribution is off
regressions: If a student can't hold stance, check shoes — some trainers have too much grip and hide bad weight distribution
Tall students tend to crouch — keep reminding: upright, not smaller
observations: Watch for students whose stance collapses the moment they throw a punch — they're moving from their arms, not their base
